  "text": "Every Thursday, Ruth found a pear on her desk.

It came from the tree outside the records office, where Leonard, the caretaker, parked his bicycle. He picked the fruit before opening the building and left it on a folded paper towel beside her keyboard.

“You could give someone else a turn,” she told him once.

“Everyone else wants them ripe.”

Ruth liked them hard enough to crunch. This was apparently sufficient grounds for an arrangement lasting eleven years.

In October, Leonard retired. There was a supermarket cake and a card that circulated twice because someone had forgotten the evening cleaners.

Ruth gave him bicycle lights.

“Nothing wrong with mine,” he said.

“The back one’s held on with string.”

“Good string.”

The following Thursday, her desk was empty. She put her bag down where the pear usually sat.

By November, fallen fruit had softened across the path. The new caretaker swept it into a shovel. Ruth watched from her window, then went downstairs and asked whether she could borrow the stepladder.

Most of the pears were beyond her reach. She picked six, all small and green.

Leonard lived in a terrace near the railway. He answered wearing the same brown cardigan he had worn at work, though without his keys dragging one pocket lower than the other.

“These aren't ripe,” he said.

“I know.”

He moved aside to let her in.

His bicycle stood in the hall. The new rear light was fitted neatly beneath the saddle.

Ruth noticed the string wound around a hook beside the door.

Leonard followed her glance.

“Still useful,” he said."
